South African medical breakthrough patents

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......a remarkable South Africa researcher doing amazing things.

Unique Selling Point:
South African medical technology. Women in science.

Summary:
A South African physiological sciences professor at Stellenbosch University and colleagues have filed five high value, high impact international clinical technology patents:

1. Method for detecting inflammation
2. Cancer nano-biosensor
3. Method for treating Alzheimer’s disease
4. Method for treating Parkinson's disease
5. Method for treating Type 2 Diabetes

We will look at her work and focus on 2. and 3.




Further information:
Etheresia (Resia) Pretorius, current professor in the Department of Physiological Sciences at Stellenbosch University, can be considered to be one of South Africa’s top female scientists, with an NRF B-rating. She takes a future focused approach to the way she conducts her research, and is constantly striving to innovate and be at the cutting edge of medical science. Professor Pretorius is the recipient of multiple national and international scientific awards.

She and colleagues have filed five high value, high impact international clinical technology patents:

1. Method for detecting inflammation
2. Cancer nano-biosensor
3. Method for treating Alzheimer’s disease
4. Method for treating Parkinson's disease
5. Method for treating Type 2 Diabetes

We will look at her work and focus on 2. and 3.

The biosensor:
The global cancer burden is increasing rapidly in developing countries where populations continue to expand. The lack of
resources and basic health infrastructure means that most people in developing countries have no access to cancer screening, early diagnosis, treatment or palliative care. Many patients are frequently sent home to die without comfort or palliative care. It is therefore of utmost importance to develop an affordable, reliable, accurate and sensitive cancer bio-marker device to detect cancer at an early stage.Tumour markers with absolute specificity are not available and a rapid diagnostic method does not exist. This nano-biosensor is novel and more sensitive (detects antibodies at pictogram levels) and diagnosis is complete in less than a minute.

Treating Alzheimers
The use of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-binding protein (LBP) to treat Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) by reducing hypercoagulation (exaggerated blood clotting) commonly associated with this disease. According to Alzheimer’s Disease International, an estimated 46.8 million people were living with dementia in 2015, and that this number will almost double every 20
years. The same source reported the estimated total worldwide cost of dementia in 2015 was US$ 818 million, and that by 2018 dementia would become a trillion dollar disease, rising to US$ 2 trillion by 2030. Our researchers have recently shown that LBP has the potential to reverse hypercoagulation in AD, amongst other conditions. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and confocal microscopy, the researchers showed that plateletpoor-plasma from subjects with AD had a much greater propensity for hypercoagulation and for amyloidogenesis, and that these could both be reversed by LBP treatment. These data demonstrate that AD can be treated by administering LBP to patients suffering from this disease

Press Release:


Medical Innovations
A researcher at the University of Stellenbosch with a special interest in blood and red blood cells has revealed several remarkable patents. The series of innovative medical breakthroughs includes a bio sensor for the early detection of cancer and remarkable new treatments for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and Type 2 Diabetes. Carte Blanche explores this cutting edge research.


Script:


V/O:
Imagine a machine that can take a single drop of blood as test it for diseases that could be developing unnoticed in your body. Giving you advance warning that some disease like Alzheimer’s or cancer is on its way -- long before it actually starts.
LINK 1:
It sounds like science fiction, but it is not. A device that can do this already exists.
V/O:
This revolutionary world-breakthrough developed right here in South Africa is one of a series of amazing medical discoveries that have been patented by one of South Africa’s brightest researchers, Prof Resia Pretorius of Stellenbosch University. She has a special interest in blood and what it can tell us about specific diseases.
Resia:
If you go to a medical practitioner…….. in your blood.
V/O:
Pretorius’ research on blood has led her to this series of astounding patents. Especially the Bio-sensor that can detect cancer early, is a revolutionary first and could save millions of lives, especially in South Africa and the developing world, says Prof Anna-Mart Engelbrecht, a colleague of Pretorius.
Prof AM Engelbrecht
So, I have a special interest in cervical cancer….non-existing.
V/O:
It is virtually non-existant in first world countries because the cancer is detected early on. But this is not the case in the developing world and South Africa. Late detection causes millions of deaths.
Prof AM Engelbrecht
In the developing world…die from.
V/O:
And they die because their cancers are not detected early on. Pretorius’ device will make it easy to screen people in remote areas and get results and early warnings of potential cancers in minutes. It could literally save millions of lives.
LINK 2:
In her research on blood Pretorius uses normal blood tests, but she has taken it a step further.
Resia:
In addition….with these novel technologies.
V/O:
Resia Pretorius grew up with her grandparents near Plettenberg Bay and always had an interest in biology. A neighbour of theirs, Mr Ted Brown, recognized Pretoria’s potential.
Resia:
And he brought books….Stellenbosch Univeristy.
V/O:
She excelled at University and after completing a PhD she became one of South Africa’s leading researchers in the field of cell morphology and imaging, using sophisticated electron microscopes. Her work in this field has been recognized worldwide.

Eventually she started to focus on blood and inflammatory markers or molecules visible in blood. They are an indication of disease somewhere in the body.
Resia:
If you are sick….would be up-regulated.
LINK 3:
Up-regulated simply means that there are more of them present than normal.
Resia:
So in all conditions like……….before it actually presents itself.
V/O:
One of these markers is Serum Ameloid A. It increases in one’s blood when cancer is present or even just imminent.
Resia:
Now, if you have full blown….beginning to be upregulated.
V/O:
So, the presence of SAA in your blood is an early warning that something is amiss.

Using this as a basis, Pretorius then decided to create a device or a bio sensor that could detect SAA in a single drop of blood within minutes, if it worked, it would be revolutionary. Giving people access to a simple yet effective early warning system against cancer. She knew just the man to help her…

Prof Willie Perold of the Engineering Faculty had already built a bio-sensor that can detect e-coli. He says the process is actually simple...

Willie:
We have a specific material…..in the lab.
V/O:
They coat this cloth or paper with a special compound, called a biorecognition element, and also print a small electrical circuit on it.
Willie:
And the biorecognition element….…the infection.
LINK 5:
And the beauty of it all is that you would only need a single drop of blood for the test.
V/O:
Prof Wim de Villiers, Rector of the University and a co-researcher of Pretorius, says this device will make a huge difference because current blood testing for markers like SAA requires time and sophisticated testing facilities.
Wim:
At present….days or so to come back.
V/O:
Pretorius’ biosensor will give results in minutes. Bio-sensors to test for other compounds in blood have already been developed and they come in the form of portable devices. This means Pretorius’ blood screening could be done easily in really remote locations.

But her work on inflammatory markers has led her to register 4 more patents: a biosensor to assess platelets in blood, and new methods to treat Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and Type 2 Diabetes by reducing abnormal blood clotting.

Patenting treatments and devices based on academic research by Universities is also fairly new in South Africa. De Villiers as rector of the University supports this trend.
Wim:
It definitely will be a trend and should be a trend….contribute to financial security.
LINK 8;
Pretorius says that her patented treatments of inflammation-linked diseases still have to undergo clinical trials.
V/O:
It could thus take a number of years before the treatments become available. However, the biosensor that can detect cancer early should be available and begin to change lives as early as the end of next year.
